title: Your AI agent keeps reshaping your game's data. How do you keep players' save files from breaking?
author: shanebrumback
selftext:
Something I keep running into with AI-built browser games: the agent happily renames fields, restructures inventories, or changes how unlocks are stored whenever it touches a feature. That's fine during development, but once real players have progress saved in localStorage or on a server, one of those refactors quietly wipes or corrupts their saves.

What I've started doing is telling the agent up front that the save format is a contract: it has a version number, changes need a migration from the previous version, and loading an old save is something it has to test before calling a feature done.

Curious how others handle it:

1. Do you version your save data from day one, or only once players complain?
2. Do you let the agent write migrations, or do you handle that part yourself?
3. Where do you keep saves for a browser game: localStorage, IndexedDB, a backend, or player accounts?
4. Has an AI refactor ever wiped player progress on you? How did you catch it?

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: Opus 5.5 is really good about doing save file migrations, in fact it’s almost too good because it’s always trying to do them when I’m still doing rapid prototyping and I have to tell it to not bother.

comments.author: mechatui
comments.body: You learn software engineering and about migrations or you just out what your wrote into Claude and you ask Claude to write a skill for it to check and make sure stuff is migrated or only to change player data if required. Saves have versions etc it should be able to tell you

comments.author: Shalke97
comments.body: My game is on save-game version 131 or something. As Seasaw mentioned, opus is really good at making it's own system. You guys really need to learn to communicate with your AI better.

comments.author: jkosciusko
comments.body:
First why is it reshaping the data? You could prevent this in a [claude.md](http://claude.md) or agents md file.  Aside from that lets suppose you absolutely need to reshape the data.  In this case you must create an adapter that allows the old data to still work.

Maybe its missing pieces that are required in the updated version? Then you will need flags that say they have old version so function as the old version.  Offer a prompt on screen to convert to new version and give the pros/cons.

What agent are you using? sounds like a lower tier model.

1. Never ever ever let issues get the users, never let them complain... this is rule number 1 in all software development. If it gets here, you get negative reviews/ratings which prevents others from even wanting to try your product.
2. Agents are good enough to do this, just do it with a decent model, no qwen here please.
3. irrelevant
4. No, tests... write tests around the most important pieces.  in Agents md say something like "If a test must change to pass verify this with me first" etc etc.

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
I would version saves from the moment real players can keep progress, but I prefer putting the version in the **filename**, for example `gamedata_v1.dat`, `gamedata_v2.dat`, rather than putting a version field inside one save file and building an increasingly complicated migration loader.

When the format changes, I keep the old loader unchanged, create a new loader for the new format, and try the newest save first before falling back to older versions. I also do not overwrite the old save when writing the new format. That gives you a recovery path if an AI refactor or bad release writes corrupted data. The agent can absolutely write the new loader, but I would make loading older real save files part of the automated tests before the change is accepted.

This is also the sort of architectural rule I like putting into the agent instructions so it cannot casually reshape persistent data. I made a free coding skill around these kinds of Data Oriented Design rules:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: I have a whole chapter on save and load architecture, versioning, backwards compatibility, and preserving old loaders in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*:

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body:
Two options:  
\- Data migrations  
\- Versioning

I personally prefer versioning.  What this means is your players can only be guaranteed to be safe using a save on a specific version of the game.  If the game updates, you do not guarantee safety of old save states.

You must keep track of versions either way, if you have migrations you must know that your data must be migrated from version x to version y.

Data migrations are a special job that gets run to convert an old style savestate to the new standard.  Given you're doing a browser based game maybe this is your only option.

Migrations are a bane in software engineering.  It's not possible to test every possible side effect of every possible data state translation from the beginning of time to current.  One slightly incorrect migration can put data in a state where it's no longer possible to get newly created data into that format, and therefore any automated tests which rely on a data state constructed with the new system cannot be guaranteed to be reliable.

Migrations aren't always avoidable, they're a necessary evil in lots of software projects.

If you must do migrations:

\- Do everything you can to never touch data stored in the save state.  
\- Every time you must touch any type of data stored in save states, create a migration script to migrate data from the previous version to the current version  
\- Seperate every migration script which migrates data from an old version to a new version, you can "safely" migrate data from an old version to a new version by running each migration script in between those versions one after another  
\- periodically evaluate whether customer data has become "impossible" to create using current data writing standards, and create migration scripts to "rectify" the impossible data into conformity with the updated standard.

comments.author: Candid-Fudge-4015
comments.body: Versioning from day one is the right call imo. Once real players exist I'd let the agent propose migrations but review them yourself, and keep a folder of real old saves from every version that each change has to load cleanly. That folder catches way more than any prompt does. For server-side saves, table history also lets you roll back a bad deploy instead of losing progress. We built that into Pixeltable, example here: [github.com/pixeltable/pixeltable/blob/main/docs/release/howto/cookbooks/core/version-control-history.ipynb](https://github.com/pixeltable/pixeltable/blob/main/docs/release/howto/cookbooks/core/version-control-history.ipynb)
